power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: The longitudinal relationship between motor and language skills at two, four and seven years of age in a large Singaporean cohort
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
Children whose motor skills develop faster have been shown to have better language skills (e.g., Gonzalez, Alvarez, Nelson, 2019 for a review). However, there are many unknowns when it comes to the reasons for this effect, as well as its robustness. First, a small number of studies exist on this subject, and to our knowledge, only one of a large cohort dataset (Wang et al., 2015), the rest on small observational or lab samples. Second, it is not clear whether this relationship exists only concurrently and in the early stages of development (up to around 2 years of age) or whether infants who develop motor skills early keep their language advantage during childhood. This relationship might stem from one or more external factors, such as maternal sensitivity or the child’s attention skills rather than from a direct effect of motor development on language skills.
We therefore aim to explore the following two hypotheses in a large sample of children growing up in Singapore (as specified in 8):
Correlations between motor and language skills will be evident in early language development (2 years of age for language, measures derived from data 2 years and younger for motor development).
While language and motor skills seem to be concurrently related at infancy, we will also examine if early motor development predicts language at 4-7 years of age when controlling for language skills at 2 years.That is – are correlations between language skills and motor development stable or are they evident only at infancy? If motor skills still predict language skills at 4 and 4.5 years of age when controlling for early language skills, this would already rule out the third-factor explanations discussed above as a sole cause for the relationship between motor and language skills, and suggest a causal link between motor and language development. If they also do so at 7 years of age then we can conclude there is evidence for even more long term effects.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Children’s language skills assessed at 2-, 4-, and 4.5-years of age measured using the following measures: 
Age 2: Communication subscale from the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, 3rd Edition (ASQ-3®, Squires et al., 2009), Receptive and Expressive Communication subscales from the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (version III, BSID-III, Bayley, 2006), Singapore Communicative Development Inventory (SCDI) adapted from the MacArthur Communicative Development Inventories
(Fenson et al., 1993). 
 Age 4: Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT-4, Dunn & Dunn, 2007) 
Age 4.5 Verbal subscale from the Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, second edition (KBIT-2, Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004).
Age 7: IQ Verbal Subset from Wechsler abbreviated scale of intelligence–second edition (WASI-II, Wechsler, 2011)	

To ensure that the scores from the different questionnaires have the same weight in our analyses, each test score will be transformed into a z score. Thus, in our statistical analyses, we will use the z transformed outcome scores at each testing age: the average score of z transformed ASQ-3, BSID-III, and SCDI scores at age two, z transformed PPVT scores at age four, z transformed KBIT-2 scores at age four and a half, and z transformed WASI-II scores at 7-years.

Another dependent variable will be Children’s performance at Novel Word Delayed Recognition Task and Novel Word Learning Task measured at 4.5-years of age -  but since these scores are not normed or validated, this analysis will be exploratory.
table.study_design_overview:
This is an observational study involving a survey, and participants were not assigned to any conditions. The same measures were obtained for all participants.
We do have key independent variables which will serve as predictors in our analyses:

Gross and fine motor skills: This will be assessed using the Gross Motor and Fine Motor subscales from ASQ-3 questionnaire administered at 9,18, and 24-months of age. These scores will be transformed to z scores and average z score will be used in analyses.
 
Control variables include: the target child’s sex, birth weight (kg), gestational age (weeks), age at testing, language of test administration, number of older siblings, maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy (grams/day), maternal smoking status at the 26th week of pregnancy, breastfeeding duration, early maternal stress (measured at infants’ age of 3 and 12 months), maternal education (six categories: no education, primary, secondary,ITE/NITEC, GCE (polytechnic/diploma), university (bachelor/masters/PhD), paternal education, maternal age at delivery (years), and paternal age at delivery. These data were collected from obstetrical records (gestational age and birth weight) and from questionnaires administered to the parents.
table.statistical_tests:
In order to ensure that the scores from the different questionnaires have the same weight in our analyses, each test score will be transformed into a z score. Thus, in our statistical analyses, we used the z transformed outcome scores at each testing age: the average score of z transformed ASQ-3 and BSID-III , and CDI scores at age two, z transformed PPVT scores at age four, z transformed KBIT-2 scores at age four and a half, z transformed WASI-II score at age 7. First, we will fit four linear models, one for each testing age (two, four,four and a half, and seven years) with the child’s precise age at testing and with aforementioned control variables but without predictors. In case of missing values, we will use the Multivariate Imputation via Chained Equations method from R package mice (Van Buuren, & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) as a principled way to predict missing values from observed values. Next, residuals will be extracted from these models and combined into one dataset to use in our main analysis to explain any residual variance left after adjusting for our control variables. Thus, in main analyses will use adjusted language scores.

Adjustment models with controlling variables:
Age 2: Lang_skills_2_adjusted = lm (Lang_skills_2~ Sex + Alcohol + Smoking + Birth_weight + Gestational_age + Exact_testing_age + Number of Older Siblings + Breasfeeding duration + Early Maternal Stress + Maternal_delivery_age + Paternal_delivery_age + Maternal_education +Paternal_education + Test_Admin_language +(1|Participants)
Age 4: Lang_skills_4_adjusted =lm (Lang_skills_4 ~ Sex + Alcohol + Smoking + Birth_weight + Gestational_age + Exact_testing_age + Number of Older Siblings + Breasfeeding duration + Early Maternal Stress + Maternal_delivery_age + Paternal_delivery_age + Maternal_education +Paternal_education + Test_Admin_language +(1|Participants)
Age 4.5: Lang_skills_4_5_adjusted = lm (Lang_skills_4_5 ~ Sex + Alcohol + Smoking + Birth_weight + Gestational_age + Exact_testing_age + Number of Older Siblings +  Breasfeeding duration + Early Maternal Stress + Maternal_delivery_age + Paternal_delivery_age + Maternal_education +Paternal_education + Test_Admin_language +(1|Participants)
Age 7: Lang_skills_7_adjusted = lm (Lang_skills_7 ~ Sex + Alcohol + Smoking + Birth_weight + Gestational_age + Exact_testing_age + Number of Older Siblings +  Breasfeeding duration + Early Maternal Stress + Maternal_delivery_age + Paternal_delivery_age + Maternal_education +Paternal_education + Test_Admin_language +(1|Participants)

Analysis 1: Relation between concurrent motor and language skills
We will fit the linear regression model with adjusted language score at 24-months as a dependent variable and Gross Motor Skill and Fine Motor Skill as predictors. This model will be fitted using the R built-in function lm (R core team, 2020). The significance of models will be assessed using Satterthwaite’s method using the anova function of the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). As a measure of effect size, Cohen’s d will be calculated from the F-statistic using the function F_to_d from the package effectsize (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020). Additionally, in order to evaluate the evidence for the null hypotheses, Bayes Factors (BFs) will be determined using the marginal likelihoods (bridgesampling) method. In order to interpret the BFs, the conventional cut-offs based on Jeffreys (1998) will be used, with a BF greater than 3 representing sufficient evidence for the experimental hypothesis, and a BF less than .33 representing sufficient evidence for the null hypothesis. BFs with values between .33 and 3 indicate that the data are inconclusive. BFs will be determined using the functions bayesfactor_models and brm from the R packages bayestestR (Makowski, et al., 2019) and brms (Bürkner, 2017). Using the function get_priors from brms package (Bürkner, 2017) we will identify the parameters that can have the priors. Next, using the function set_priors from the same package the priors will be defined by using the Cauchy distribution (0, 0.7) based on Schönbrodt et al. (2017).  Here, the missing data will not be imputed, but in cases where a child is missing language scores at 2-years of age, the child will be excluded from analysis.

Main model:
Model 1 <- lm (Lang_skills_2_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill)

Bayes models:
B1 <- brm (Lang_skills_2_adjusted ~ 1, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B2 <- brm (Lang_skills_2_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B3 <- brm (Lang_skills_2_adjusted ~ Fine Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B4 <- brm (Lang_skills_adjusted_2 ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)

Model comparison:
bayesfactor_models(B1, B2, B3, B4, denominator=1)

Analysis 2: Relation between children’s early motor skills and later language development
To assess the relation between children’s motor skills and later language development, we will run two linear regression models. The first model will assess the relation between children’s motor skills and language development at 4- to-4.5-years of age while controlling for language skills at 2-years. Thus, the model will be run with the adjusted language scores (averaged for 4 and 4.5 years of age) as the dependent variable, Gross Motor Skill and Fine Motor Skill as between-subject independent variables, and adjusted language scores at 2-years as a control variable. 
The second model will assess the relation between children’s motor skills and language development at 7-years of age while controlling for language skills at 2-years. Thus, the model will be run with the adjusted language scores at 7 years of age as the dependent variable, Gross Motor Skill and Fine Motor Skill as between-subject independent variables, and adjusted language scores at 2-years as control variable. 
The models will be fitted using the R built-in function lm (R core team, 2020). Here, the missing data will not be imputed, but in cases where a child is missing language scores at a targeted age, the child will be excluded from analysis. Significance of the model, effect sizes, and Bayes factors will be obtained in the same way as in Analysis 1.

Motor development and language skills at 4-years:
Model 2 <- lm (Language_skills_4_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill + Language_skills_2)

Bayes models:
B1 <- brm (Lang_skills_4_adjusted ~ 1, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B2 <- brm (Lang_skills_4_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B3 <- brm (Lang_skills_4_adjusted ~ Fine Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B4 <- brm (Lang_skills_4_adjusted ~ Language_skills_2, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B5 <- brm (Lang_skills_4_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill + Language_skills_2, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)

Model comparison:
bayesfactor_models(B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, denominator=1)

Motor development and language skills at 7-years:
Model 3 <- lm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill + Language_skills_2)

Bayes models:
B1 <- brm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ 1, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B2 <- brm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B3 <- brm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ Fine Motor Skill, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B4 <- brm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ Language_skills_2, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)
B5 <- brm (Lang_skills_7_adjusted ~ Gross Motor Skill + Fine Motor Skill + Language_skills_2, prior = prior, save_all_pars = TRUE)

table.outliers_and_exclusions: Children with no reported Gross and Fine Motor data on ASQ-3 assessment at all three ages 9-, 18-, and 24-months will be excluded. In Analysis 1, children with no language score at 24-months will be excluded, whereas in analysis 2 children with no language scores at both 4- and 4.5-years (Model 2) and children with no language data at 7-years (Model 3) will be excluded as well as children with no scores at 2-years of age (in both Model 2 and Model 3).
table.sample_size: In this study, we are using a sample from Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes (GUSTO), a population based birth cohort study from Singapore (Soh et al., 2014). This cohort consists of 1176 children, however, participants who do not fulfill our exclusion criteria will be excluded (see above for exclusion criteria). We will therefore know the exact sample size only after posting this preregistration, but expect it to be around 1000 children for each analysis.
table.additional_comments:
The data we analyze is derived from the GUSTO cohort dataset in Singapore, see Soh et
al., (2014) for details about this dataset. The authors who are deriving the hypotheses and conducting analyses for this preregistered project (IL, NH, ST) have not been implicated in the data collection. They have accessed most of the data to look at a different question (Havron et al., 2022) but have not looked at the data in light of the present hypotheses. We will gain access to the full data after posting this preregistration.

The emerging abilities of infants and children shape how they interact with others and the world around them.
Two key developmental abilities are motor and language skills.

While the development of these two abilities has often been assessed separately, there is reason to believe that they do not develop in isolation but might be related, such that motor abilities support the development of language abilities (Gonzalez et al., 2019; Iverson, 2021).

text.text: Examining how these abilities interact could lead to novel insights into factors such as the source of developmental boosts and individual differences in development.
The interaction between motor and language skills could happen through two major routeswhich we will refer to as the physical and developmental cascades routes in the following.
The physical route could promote language development because speech requires coordinated, controlled and timed movement of the articulatory organs.
Oral-motor skills are related to fine-motor skills, which are the skills to control and coordinate small muscles in movement, such as those in the hands and fingers (Newmeyer, et al., 2007).

text.text: Oral-motor skills such as those used in language production are related to speeded tasks that require precision grip (Brookman et al., 2013) -perhaps because the oral skills required for speech are also speeded, coordinated and precise.

text.text: The physical route could also affect language development by shaping neural pathways associated with motor skills.

text.text: Gross motor skills (using large muscles in the torso, legs, and arms for whole-body movements like sitting and walking) are also related to speech production.

For example, upright position (sitting or standing) makes it easier for infants to produce sounds by enabling infants to breathe more deeply, maintain subglottal pressure, and affect the curve of the vocal cords (Yingling, 1981).

text.text: Motor skills might also contribute to language development via another route, the developmental cascades route.
According to this theory, motor skills enable an infant a more proactive relationship with their environment (Iverson, 2010 (Iverson, , 2021)).

text.text: Interactions with parents are then changed by the new way the infant interacts with their environment, creating a cascade of developmental processes.

Indeed, parents have been found to talk more, and differently, to walking than to crawling infants aged 9 to 15 months (Karasik et al., 2011; Schneider & Iverson, 2022). Walle (2016) showed that walking experience is associated with more infant initiation of joint engagement, as well as gaze following -that is, walking is associated with more proactive relationships with the environment, which in turn can lead to more occasions for caregivers to (verbally) respond to infants of 10-to 13 months. He et al. (2015) found that walking American and Chinese 12-to 14-month-old infants had larger vocabularies than crawling infants of the same age.

text.text: Unlike for gross motor skills, the link between fine motor skills and caregiver interactions is less intuitive.

One suggestion is that advanced fine motor skills might enable the child to manipulate toys for a longer time period giving parents more to talk about during play time, as parents' utterances were found to contain a significantly greater proportion of labels relative to moments when infants (aged 10 to 14 months) were not holding objects (West & Iverson, 2017).

text.text: This suggestion, however, highlights the challenge of discriminating between the effect of fine and gross-motor skills on language development at this age: Infant sitting frees up their hands to manipulate objects and gesture, and so, it is a combination of both fine and gross motor skills that would be related to language development.

Gestures themselves are an invaluable part of the development of language and communication (e.g., Longobardi et al., 2014), and have been shown to not only predate but also predict changes in language, suggesting that early gesture may be paving the way for future developments in language (Iverson & Goldin-Meadow, 2005).

text.text: Additionally, because most studies are cross-sectional, a concurrent relationship between motor and language skills may reflect other factors that positively affect both.

For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?W7nxuI infants' executive function skills might also be linked to both motor (Maurer & Roebers, 2019) and language development (Viterbori et al., 2012) , and it has been found that they tap into joint resources, such that there exists an interference effect between motor and cognitive activities at 12 months of age (Boudreau & Bushnell, 2000).

text.text: If such a third factor is at play, then the observed relation found between motor and language skills might be an artifact of other confounding factors rather than evidence for a true contribution of motor development to language development.
The state of the literature leaves several unanswered questions.
The major question is how robust and generalizable the relation between motor and language skills is, given the limitations of samples and methods previously used.
The second question is whether fine or gross motor skills, or both, relate to language acquisition.
The third is whether this relation exists only concurrently, or whether infants who develop motor skills early keep their language-skills advantage during childhood.
First, for the question of robustness, there are not enough large, longitudinal studies to be able to assess such robustness.
Moreover, as far as we could tell, almost all studies were performed on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) samples.
One study was performed in China (He et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?45xOoD 2015) and one in East Asia and the Pacific (Zhang et al., 2018) , focusing on older children.

text.text: The GUSTO cohort is particularly valuable due to its large size, longitudinal design, collection of demographic, perinatal, and parental factors, and ethnically diverse population.
This cohort includes more than 1,000 children and has data on motor development at 9, 18, and 24 months, and on language development at 9, 18, and 24 months and at 4 to 4.5 years of age.
We addressed three research questions.
First, are motor and language skills concurrently associated in a large, non-WEIRD population cohort?
We hypothesized that fine and gross motor skills would each be associated with language at 9, 18, and 24 months.
Second, do motor skills predict later language over and above earlier language skills?
We hypothesized that motor skills would predict language from 9 to 18 months, 18 to 24 months, and 24 months to 4-4.5 years.
Third, do fine and gross motor skills differ in their relation to language?
We expected both to be related to language, but made no prediction about their relative strength.
The children were born between November 30, 2009 and May 1, 2011, and data collection is still ongoing.
Participants all had a homogeneous parental ethnic background, following the CMIO model (Chinese-Malay-Indian-Others) commonly used in Singapore.
At study onset, 56.1% of participants were Chinese, 25.4% Malay, and 18.5% Indian.
For the study, we included children with data on our variables of interest in at least one time point: 9 months, 18 months, 24 months, and 48-to 54 months.
Two hundred twenty-nine participants had data at all time points, 175 had data at three time points, 239 had data at 2 time points, and 242 had data at one time point.
Overall, data from 885 children were analyzed (see Table 1 for sample size for each individual time point and measure).

text.text: It specified a cross-lagged panel model from 9 months to 4-4.5 years, and the first submission of this manuscript was based on it (Supplementary Material 3).
Two features of the planned analysis differ from the analysis reported below.
First, language scores were residualized on the demographic and perinatal covariates before entering the model.
Second, at 24 months and 4-4.5 years, scores from the available language measures were z-transformed and averaged into composites.

During peer review, reviewers pointed out that residualizing only the language outcomes adjusts the two domains unequally, and that it removes covariate-related stability from the autoregressive paths.
They also noted that equal-weight composites assume the instruments are equally reliable and valid.
We agreed with both points.
Covariates are now included directly in the structural equation model as predictors of all motor and language variables.
Language at 24 months and at 4-4.5 years is now modeled as a latent factor with freely estimated loadings.
We therefore do not consider the analysis reported here to be preregistered.
The concurrent associations and the comparison of fine-with grossmotor effects were also not preregistered predictions.
All three analyses found consistent concurrent associations between motor and language skills.
Both cross-lagged analyses found only one significant longitudinal motor-to-language path, but they disagreed on which path it was (Supplementary Material 3).

text.text: The KBIT-2 is an individually administered assessment of intellectual ability normed for ages 4 to 90.
Although this battery results in three scores: a verbal score, a non-verbal score, and an IQ composite, here, only the verbal score was used.
The verbal scale is itself made up of two subtests, Verbal Knowledge and Riddles.
Verbal Knowledge is receptive: the examiner says a word or asks about a general-information concept and the child points to the picture that best fits.
In the Riddles subscale, the examiner gives several verbal clues about a concept, and the child identifies a word that fits all conditions.
The KBIT-2 shows good reliability and validity (Singer, et al., 2012).

text.text: All statistical analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2020).

Language and motor variables (ASQ Communication, BSID-III, PPVT, KBIT) were entered into the model as their original z-scores from the dataset, each standardized within wave on the full available sample for that instrument.

The PPVT (administered at 48 months) and the KBIT-2 verbal subtest (administered at 54 months) were treated as two language measures available at 4 to 4.5 years, and (as at all ages with two available measures) were combined into a latent language factor (described below).

Continuous covariates (gestational age, birth weight, parental ages, breastfeeding duration, maternal and paternal education, maternal anxiety and depression) and age-at-testing variables were standardized before entering the SEM to ensure numerical stability.
All standardization was conducted on the full analytic sample prior to model fitting.
We used no imputation; FIML handled all missing data directly.

To examine the developmental relationship between motor and language skills, we implemented a cross-lagged panel model using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) and plotted with DiagrammeR (Iannone & Roy, 2026).

text.text: This approach allowed us to simultaneously model autoregressive paths (stability within domains over time), cross-domain effects (influences from one domain to another over time), and within-time covariances (concurrent relations between domains).
The model included both fine and gross motor measures at 9, 18, and 24 months, and language measures at 9, 18, 24 months, and 4-to-4.5 years.
Specifically, our model estimated: autoregressive paths for motor and language skills, cross-domain effects from motor to language skills, and within-time covariances between domains.
Fine and gross motor skills were allowed to covary within each wave but not across waves.
At time points where multiple language instruments were available, we specified latent language factors.

At 24 months, a latent factor was defined by the ASQ Communication subscale and the BSID-III Language scale, with the ASQ loading fixed to 1 for identification, and the BSID-III loading freely estimated.
At four to four and a half years, a latent factor was defined by the PPVT and the KBIT-2 verbal subtest, with the PPVT loading fixed to 1.
This approach allows the data to determine the relative contribution of each instrument and partitions measurement error into indicatorspecific residual variances.
At 9 and 18 months, only the ASQ Communication subscale was available, so the observed score was used directly.
Residual covariances between examiner-administered instruments across waves (BSID-III at 24 months with PPVT and KBIT at four to four and a half years) were included.
Demographic and perinatal covariates were included as predictors of each observed variable and latent factor at every wave.

The covariates were: sex, alcohol consumption during pregnancy, smoking during pregnancy, birth weight, gestational age, number of siblings, breastfeeding duration, maternal anxiety (STAI, 3 months postpartum), maternal depression (EPDS, 3 months postpartum), maternal and paternal age at delivery, and maternal and paternal education.
Age at testing was included as a predictor of each variable at its corresponding wave, with separate age variables for the ASQ covariation (standardized cov = 0.350, p < .001).

text.text: These standardized covariances reflect small to moderate concurrent relations between domains at each timepoint.

Fine motor skills at 9 months showed a marginal association with language skills at 18 months (standardized β = 0.110, p = .054), representing a small effect that did not reach conventional significance.
Gross motor skills at 9 months did not significantly predict language skills at 18 months (standardized β = 0.063, p = .273).

At 18 months, fine motor skills did not significantly predict language at 24 months (standardized β = 0.074, p = .242), but gross motor skills at 18 months significantly predicted language at 24 months (standardized β = 0.151, p = .004), representing a small effect.

For the final developmental period, neither fine motor skills (standardized β = 0.087, p = .143) nor gross motor skills (standardized β = -0.070, p = .205) at 24 months significantly predicted language at four to four and a half years (see Figure 1 and Table 2).

text.text: Note that the only significant cross-time cross-domain effect (gross motor skills at 18 months predicting language at 24 months) involves the ASQ parental questionnaire as both a motor and language measure, raising the concern that the effect is primarily driven by shared-instrument bias.
To address this concern, we ran the model again, replacing the latent language factor at 24 months with only the examiner-administered BSID-III language score.
This model showed somewhat reduced fit (CFI = 0.917, RMSEA = 0.053, SRMR = 0.035), likely because replacing the latent factor with a single indicator removes measurement error modeling.

Nonetheless, gross motor skills at 18 months continued to significantly predict BSID-III language scores at 24 months (standardized β = 0.084, p = .040), albeit with a smaller effect size than in the main model, suggesting that the cross-lagged effect is not driven solely by shared-instrument bias.

This model also yielded a significant path from fine motor skills at 24 months to language at four to four and a half years (standardized β = 0.119, p = .047) that was not significant in the main model; given the reduced model fit, this result should be interpreted cautiously.

text.text: To examine whether fine-or gross-motor skills were more strongly related to language outcomes, we ran Wald tests to compare the strength of the relationship at each timepoint.

For the concurrent within-time covariances, fine motor skills showed a significantly stronger association with language than gross motor skills at 18 months (χ²(1) = 7.25, p = .007), with a similar, non-significant, trend at 24 months (χ²(1) = 2.89, p = .089).
At 9 months, the concurrent associations of fine motor and gross motor skills with communication were not significantly different (χ²(1) = 0.62, p = .430).
No significant differences were found for cross-lagged paths (see Table 2).

text.text: Although fine motor skills showed a marginal association with language at 9-18 months while gross motor skills reached significance at 18-24 months, the effect sizes were comparable in magnitude and not statistically distinguishable, suggesting that this pattern reflects sampling variability rather than a meaningful difference between motor domains.

To examine the impact of our covariate adjustment, we also estimated the model without covariates or age-at-testing controls.
The unadjusted model showed acceptable fit (χ²(38) = 72.463, p = .001, CFI = 0.964, RMSEA = 0.056, SRMR = 0.074).
The significant cross-lagged path from the adjusted model remained significant without covariates: gross motor at 18 months predicted language at 24 months (β = 0.157, p = .007).

The fine motor at 9 months path, which was marginal in the adjusted model, reached significance without covariates (β = 0.114, p = .046), suggesting that its attenuation in the adjusted model partly reflects shared variance with demographic and perinatal factors.

However, the unadjusted model also showed an additional path that did not survive covariate adjustment: fine motor at 24 months showed a marginal association with language at four to four and a half years (β = 0.130, p = .051).

The attenuation of this path after controlling for demographic, perinatal, and maternal variables suggests it partly reflects shared variance with confounding factors rather than a direct developmental effect.
The current state of the literature on the relation between motor and language development leaves several unanswered questions.
The main question is how robust and generalizable the effect of motor development on language outcomes is, given the methodological limitations of previous studies.
The second question is whether it is fine or gross motor skills, or both, that are related to language acquisition.
The third is whether this relation exists only concurrently or whether infants who develop motor skills early preserve their language-skills advantage during childhood.

Regarding the first question, our findings provide evidence for robust concurrent relations between motor and language skills, replicating previous findings (e.g., Andalò et al., 2022; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014) in a new cultural context with a large population cohort, while controlling for multiple potential confounding factors.

text.text: Within-time covariances showed significant associations between motor and language skills at all time points for which we had data on both areas.

Regarding the second question of whether fine or gross motor skills are more strongly related to language development, our results suggest that fine motor skills may show more consistent relations with language outcomes concurrently, but we found no evidence that fine motor skills were more strongly related to language than gross motor skills were longitudinally.

Specifically, our analysis found that fine motor skills at 9 months significantly predicted language skills at 18 months, while gross motor skills at 18 months predicted language skills at 24 months, however, the size of the effect of fine and gross motor skills on language at both these time points was not significantly different.

Concurrently, fine motor skills were more closely related to language than were gross motor skills at 18 months of age, but not at 9 months of age, and the results were marginal, though not significant, at 24 months of age.

This pattern aligns with theoretical frameworks emphasizing the physical route between motor and language development (Brookman et al., 2013; Gaines & Missiuna, 2007), particularly given that the 18-month language assessment includes substantial motor components (production and gestural communication comprising two-thirds of the items).

text.text: However, the equal weight of fine-and gross-motor skills at 9 months is surprising, since most items on the language assessment at 9 months focused on language production.

Regarding the third question of whether relations are concurrent versus predictive, our findings suggest that motor-language associations are primarily concurrent rather than reflecting long-term developmental cascades.
When controlling for potential confounding variables, only one out of six cross-domain longitudinal paths was significant -the effect of gross motor skills at 18 months on language at 24 months.
Fine motor skills at 9 months had only a marginal, non-significant effect on language at 18 months.
No significant cross-domain effects were observed at the later developmental period.
The finding that both significant and marginal cross-lagged paths occurred between early time points warrants consideration.
These findings mirror Oudgenoeg-Paz et al. (2016), who found that age of walking did not directly predict language at age 43 months.

text.text: One interpretation is that motorlanguage cascades are genuinely limited to the first two years, when motor and communicative development are most rapidly co-developing.
During this period, motor advances open new opportunities for social interaction and exploration that may scaffold language acquisition.

Fine motor control at 9 months supports gesture and object manipulation that elicits caregiver labeling (West & Iverson, 2017), while gross motor advances at 18 months such as stable walking expand the child's capacity for initiating joint attention and accessing new communicative contexts (Walle, 2016; Karasik et al., 2011).

text.text: By 24 months, when motor competence is more established and language development is increasingly driven by linguistic input and cognitive factors, the direct contribution of motor skills may diminish.
However, an important consideration in interpreting these developmental trajectories is the nature of the language measures across time points.

The language assessments at 18 and 24 months included both comprehension and production components (ASQ Communication at both time points and Bayley Language scales at 24 months), while the 4-to-4.5 years assessments focused on receptive vocabulary and verbal reasoning abilities rather than speech production (PPVT and KBIT verbal subtests).

The absence of cross-domain effects in the later developmental period may reflect this shift from mixed comprehension-production measures to purely receptive language abilities, suggesting that any motor-language connections may be more pronounced for expressive rather than receptive language skills.

If this is the case, then it is not necessarily that the relations between motor and language skills shift across developmental stages, but that, lacking a measure of language production at later ages, we fail to detect the relation between fine motor skills and language production at later stages of development.

While statistical tests found no significant differences between the size of the relationship of language skills and fine-and gross-motor skills, it is worth considering why it was fine motor skills at 9 months which marginally predicted language at 18 months, and gross-motor skills which predicted language at 24 months.
One possibility has to do with the nature of the questions asked of parents in the fine-and gross-motor subscales.

As we mention in the introduction, sitting is one gross-motor milestone which is considered important by the developmental cascades theory, as infant sitting frees up their hands to manipulate objects and gesture. Libertus & Violi (2016) found a relationship between the development of sitting skills around five months of age and language skills at 10 and 14 months of age.

text.text: However, manipulating objects and gesturing (which sitting allows for) would be considered finemotor skills.
In the ASQ the parents filled in for our current study, at 9 months, parents are asked about manipulating and picking up objects in the fine-motor subscale.
Only one question in the gross-motor subscale related to sitting, with the others focusing on standing (except one about cruising) -which might be less relevant to language development.
The fine-motor scale will therefore be more relevant according to the developmental cascades theory.
At 18 months, half of the gross-motor questions were about walking, which is also considered a significant gross-motor milestone in the developmental cascades theory.
The fine motor questions however, focus on more precise grip and hand-eye coordination, such as "Does your child get a spoon into her mouth right side up so that the food usually doesn't spill?".
At 18 months, therefore, the gross-motor subscale was more relevant to the developmental cascades theory.

While it is tempting to interpret these results in line with the developmental cascades model, the relationship between language and these two motor areas is statistically indistinguishable in both ages, and so these findings might represent sampling variability rather than a meaningful difference between motor domains.
Finally, when we reran our analysis without controlling for confounding factors, the pattern of cross-domain effects shifted subtly.

The fine motor at 9 months path, which was marginal in the adjusted model, crossed the significance threshold without covariates, despite the effect sizes being nearly identical -illustrating the fragility of relying on conventional significance cutoffs alone.
Fine motor skills at 24 months also showed a marginal association with language at four to four and a half years that did not approach significance in the adjusted model.
These shifts highlight the importance of controlling for potential confounds, as shared risk and protective factors may create spurious associations between motor and language development.
For instance, executive function skills are linked to both motor (Maurer & Roebers, 2019) and language development (Viterbori et al., 2012).

text.text: Similarly, when we replaced the latent language factor at 24 months with only the examineradministered BSID-III, a significant path from fine motor skills at 24 months to language at four to four and a half years emerged.
This could be because we were now modeling a path from an examineradministered tool to an examiner-administered tool.
This is another important methodological point to consider when interpreting our results.
However, given the reduced model fit in that analysis, this result should be interpreted cautiously.
These findings do not negate the importance of motor development for overall child development, but they do suggest that interpretations of direct causal relations should be made with care.
The current study has several important limitations that constrain our ability to draw strong causal conclusions.
First, the only measure used to asses infants' motor development was the ASQ, which is a parental report which only includes six questions per motor area.

The ASQ may be more appropriate for screening purposes than for assessing individual differences, given that at 18 months 61.8% of children scored the maximum, and at 24 months 49.4% scored the maximum.
This ceiling effect can reduce variance and may have attenuated the cross-lagged estimates for gross motor at these waves.
Second, at 18 and 24 months both language and motor skills were assessed with subsets of the same measure, the ASQ.

At 24 months we also had access to the BSID-III as a language assessment, and our analysis showed that the relationship between gross-motor and language skills remains significant even if only the BSID-III is kept as a language measure and the ASQ is excluded.
Nonetheless, having no other language assessment other than the ASQ at 18 months is a limitation.
Third, we lacked direct measures of parent-child interactions, which may serve as important mediating mechanisms in motor-language relations.

Previous research has demonstrated that motor development changes the nature of parent-child interactions, with parents talking more, and differently, to walking compared to those who are crawling (Karasik et al., 2011; Schneider & Iverson, 2022) and walking experience being associated with more infant-initiated joint engagement (Walle, 2016).

text.text: Finally, our language measures varied in their assessment focus across developmental time points, with early measures including both comprehension and production components while later measures focused on comprehension.
This measurement heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of developmental trajectories and may contribute to the absence of later cross-domain effects.

Our analysis of a large population cohort provides evidence for concurrent relations between motor and language skills, with fine-motor skills being somewhat more strongly related to language skills than are gross-motor skills.
However, our results also suggest that longitudinal motor-to-language effects are more limited, with one two out of six paths proving significant.

The finding that gross-motor skills at 18 months predict language at 24 months even when controlling for multiple confounds, are consistent with both the physical route between motor and language skills and the developmental cascades theory.
However, given that statistical tests showed no difference between the relationship of fine-and grossmotor skills and language at that timepoint, they should be interpreted with caution.
